places.summary: A speakeasy behind a cigar store: knock twice, say Joe sent you, and drink bathtub gin out of teacups.
A speakeasy in a restaurant's cellar, with a piano, a lookout at the stairs and a bell that rings when the cops come.
Rum come in off the boats at night, poured in a boathouse where the tide slaps under the floor.
Officially a soda bar; unofficially, the bellhop knows a fellow, and the ice comes with something in it.
An old saloon turned 'near-beer' parlour, where the beer is nearer than the law would like.
A members-only club of the Irish, Italian or German societies, with card tables and a very private bar.
A roadhouse out on the highway where couples drive for dancing, chicken dinners and something in the punch.
A jazz club with a hot band, a chorus line, white tablecloths and a dance floor that shakes after midnight.
A huge dance hall with two bands on two stages, taxi dancers at a dime a dance and a mirrored ball.
A dance pavilion on the water where the big bands play summer nights and the doors open to the breeze.
A Saturday rent party in a top-floor flat, a stride pianist and a quarter at the door to help with the landlord.
A cabaret where a torch singer works the room, the band plays blue and the floor show changes every Thursday.
A shiny lunch wagon by the trolley line with a counter of stools, hash, pie and coffee all night.
Put a nickel in the slot and lift a little glass door: pie, beans or a cup of coffee from a dolphin spout.
Spaghetti, red sauce, checked tablecloths and wine in coffee cups for the regulars who know to ask.
An upstairs chop suey parlour with lanterns, a dance floor and an orchestra on Saturday nights.
Pastrami piled high, pickles from the barrel and a counterman who has an opinion about everything.
Chowder, steamers and fried clams at long tables, with the fishing boats unloading right outside.
Chicken salad, little sandwiches and a string trio for ladies who have been shopping all morning.
Steak, a dance band and a floor show; the best seats go to the bootleggers and the mayor.
Ribs and hot links smoked out back over hickory, eaten off butcher paper with white bread.
Grilled cheese, tomato soup and a malted at the five-and-dime counter, the cheapest hot lunch on Main Street.
A marble soda fountain with a soda jerk flipping ice cream into egg creams, phosphates and banana splits.
Coffee and crullers for the morning crowd off the streetcar, and a booth in the back where the reporters drink.
Hot rolls at dawn, rye bread, crumb cake and a bakery truck that delivers door to door.
A tea shop for artists and poets in a basement, candles in bottles and poetry readings on Tuesday.
Doughnuts fried in the window on a new machine that draws a crowd just to watch.
Farmers' stands, fish counters and a butcher's row under a big tin roof, loud with Italian, Yiddish and Polish.
A chain grocery with tins stacked to the ceiling, coffee ground at the counter and a boy to carry your bags.
A street full of pushcarts selling pickles, socks, pots, fish and bananas, haggling in five languages.
Trucks backed up to the curb on Saturday morning with sweet corn, tomatoes, eggs and fresh-killed chickens.
Cod, haddock and lobsters sold off the boats at dawn, with the gulls fighting over the trimmings.
Six floors of escalators, perfume counters, a toy department at Christmas and the first air cooling in town.
Everything for five or ten cents: hair pins, sheet music, goldfish and a lunch counter.
Phonographs, sheet music and the new race records, with listening booths for trying before buying.
Straw boaters, two-tone shoes, silk ties and suits on credit for young men who want to look like money.
Bobs, finger waves and permanent waves under a terrifying machine, with the best gossip in town.
Crystal sets, cabinet radios and a set always playing in the window, so a crowd gathers for the ballgame.
A plate-glass showroom of new sedans and roadsters, on the installment plan, with a salesman in spats.
New novels, a rental shelf at three cents a day and a back room of books the censors haven't noticed yet.
A movie palace with a Wurlitzer organ, gilded boxes and ushers with flashlights, the newsreel and a feature for a quarter.
Vaudeville twice a day: jugglers, a dog act, a tenor, a comedy team and a headliner from the big time.
An amateur theatre company in a converted barn, putting on Ibsen and arguing about it afterwards.
The fraternal lodge hall, home to the Elks, the Moose, the Grange dances and the women's club bazaar.
A band shell in the park where the town band plays Sousa marches on summer Sunday evenings.
Boxing on Friday nights under a cloud of cigar smoke, with the local boy against whoever came in on the train.
When the chautauqua comes: a big brown tent with lectures, a Swiss bell-ringer choir and a man who saw Lincoln.
A Beaux-Arts museum given by a lumber baron, plaster casts of Greek statues and one real Rembrandt, maybe.
A museum in the old captain's house of spinning wheels, whaling harpoons and the town's first fire engine.
A mastodon skeleton, dioramas of stuffed bison and a planetarium projector that only works on Sundays.
A Carnegie library of yellow brick with a domed reading room, a children's story hour and the town's only quiet.
A private subscription library of leather armchairs and old men asleep behind newspapers.
A town park with a war memorial, a duck pond, a bandstand and benches full of old soldiers on Decoration Day.
A trolley park at the end of the line with a roller coaster, a carousel, a dance hall and a penny arcade.
A boardwalk of saltwater taffy, rolling chairs, fortune tellers and bathing beauties on parade.
Sandlot ball, swings and a wading pool where the neighbourhood children spend the whole of July.
An old rural cemetery of winding drives, weeping willows and Civil War graves, where people still come for Sunday walks.
A racetrack, a grandstand and livestock barns, empty most of the year, then the county fair in August.
A formal rose garden with a pergola, a sundial and a garden club that judges everyone else's roses.
A glass conservatory of palms, orchids and a banana tree that has actually fruited once.
Garden plots left over from the war, now full of tomatoes, sunflowers and neighbours comparing beans.
A town beach with a bathhouse, a lifeguard tower and the scandal of the new one-piece bathing suits.
A rocky cove reached by a long flight of steps, for clam bakes, picnics and moonlight swims you don't tell your mother about.
A wooden ballpark for the minor league club, with knothole gang kids and a hot dog man who throws the buns.
Saturday football in raccoon coats, pennants and hip flasks, the band marching at the half.
A wooden board track where racing cars hit a hundred miles an hour and the crowd ducks the splinters.
A YMCA with a pool, a gym with ropes and rings, a reading room and cheap rooms upstairs for young men new to town.
A boxing gym over a garage, heavy bags, skipping ropes and a trainer chewing a cigar who never says much.
A country club with nine holes, a clubhouse veranda and members who play more cards than golf.
Clay courts and white flannels, tennis teas and a ladies' tournament that half the town watches.
A roller rink with an organ playing waltzes, couples skating arm in arm and a lot of bruised knees.
A Catholic church of the parish with bingo in the basement, a big Easter and a priest who knows every family.
A white steeple on the green, church suppers, a choir and a minister who preaches against the speakeasies.
A brick church with a gospel choir that brings people in from three towns over, and a Sunday dinner after.
A synagogue with a Hebrew school, a sisterhood bake sale and a cantor whose voice fills the street on the high holy days.
Sunday services with messages from the departed, a lot of tambourines and a medium in a turban.
The town's first skyscraper, twelve storeys of terracotta with an observation floor and an elevator boy.
A lighthouse on the point with a foghorn the whole town hears on grey nights, and a keeper who welcomes visitors.
A big union station with a vaulted waiting room, a clock everyone meets under and the Twentieth Century on the board.
A steel drawbridge that goes up for the freighters, holding up the streetcars and everyone late for work.
A bronze doughboy on a granite plinth, with wreaths every Armistice Day and the names of the boys who didn't come home.
A brick mill by the falls, half of it still weaving and the other half empty since the strike.
Trawlers, schooners and lobster boats tied up three deep, the smell of bait and diesel and gulls everywhere.
Where the coastal steamers and excursion boats dock, crowded on summer Sundays with day-trippers.
Freighters, coal hoists and longshoremen who load by hand, the hiring shape-up at six every morning.
A parkway along the river where people take a Sunday drive in the new motorcar, or walk it in the old shoes.
A path along the sea cliffs past the mansions' back lawns, with the surf booming below.
A dirt road into the woods where the Boy Scouts camp, the bootleggers hide their stills and couples park.
The old interurban right of way out of town through orchards, empty since the line went bust.
Mutoscopes, fortune-telling machines, a strength tester and a mechanical gypsy who is never wrong.
A grass airfield where barnstormers give five-dollar rides on Sundays and wing-walkers draw the crowd.
The travelling carnival on the lot by the gas works: a Ferris wheel, freak show, hoochie-coochie tent and a crooked wheel of fortune.
The new craze: eighteen holes of windmills, castles and tunnels on a vacant lot, lit up till midnight.
A filling station and garage with a hand-cranked gas pump and a mechanic who can fix a Model T with wire.
Linotype machines clattering, reporters on the phones and the night edition rolling at eleven.
A radio station above the bank, broadcasting dance bands, farm prices and a preacher on Sunday morning.
Lobster boats and rum runners built side by side, and nobody asks why one needs three engines.
A vet who has gone from horses to dogs as the motorcars came in, and misses the horses.
Egg salad sandwiches, coffee and a slice of lemon meringue at a counter for office girls on their lunch hour.
A self-service cafeteria with trays, a steam table of pot roast and creamed corn, and the cheapest Sunday dinner in town.
The armory hall where the dance marathon is on: couples swaying for a week straight for a hundred-dollar prize.
Cigars, racing forms and a phone in the back where you can place a bet, if you know who to ask.
